name: vhs
why: Scripts terminal sessions into GIF recordings from a tape file; clever, but mostly a recording tool.

brief.what_it_is: VHS is a command-line tool that scripts a terminal session and records it. You write a plain-text .tape file listing commands such as Type, Enter, Sleep, Wait and Set, and VHS runs them in its own virtual terminal while capturing frames. The output is a GIF by default, and the README also lists MP4, WebM, a PNG frame directory, and .txt or .ascii text files for golden-file testing. The README also covers recording a tape from a live session (vhs record), publishing a GIF to vhs.charm.sh, and running a self-hosted SSH server.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to "Write terminal GIFs as code for integration testing and demoing your CLI tools." Keeping the demo in a versioned tape file means it can be regenerated in CI instead of being re-recorded by hand.
brief.how_it_works: Each tape command is an instruction for VHS to perform on its virtual terminal, and the README says Set commands must sit at the top of the file. The README does not explain the internals in detail, but it lists ttyd and ffmpeg as required programs that must be on PATH. Wait takes a regex and a scope (Line or Screen), and Sleep holds the recording while something like a spinner runs.

brief.install_notes: VHS needs ttyd and ffmpeg installed and available on PATH; the README's Debian/Ubuntu and Fedora/RHEL snippets say to install ttyd separately from its GitHub releases. Other install routes are pacman -S vhs, nix-env -iA nixpkgs.vhs, scoop install vhs, winget install charmbracelet.vhs, sudo xbps-install vhs, go install github.com/charmbracelet/vhs@latest, plus Debian and RPM packages and binaries from the releases page. Server mode needs an SSH key at .ssh/vhs_ed25519 by default, which the server config can override with VHS_KEY_PATH. No account is needed for local use.
brief.standout: It treats a terminal demo as a text file you can version, diff, and regenerate in CI, and the README points to a golden-file workflow where .ascii or .txt output is committed and compared between runs. Its tape language also covers Hide/Show for setup steps that stay out of the recording, plus Wait on a regex so a recording can sync with a spinner or prompt.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a latest-release badge and a build status badge, and it documents recent features such as Set Columns, Set Rows, ScrollUp/ScrollDown and Copy/Paste, but it gives no release date or last-commit date and I did not check the releases or commit pages.
brief.caveats: Requires ttyd and ffmpeg on PATH, and Windows and Linux distributions need extra setup per the README. The README warns that the SSH server gives access to the host's commands and applications, and that leaving VHS_AUTHORIZED_KEYS_PATH empty makes the server publicly accessible. Set Columns cannot be combined with Set Width, and Set Rows cannot be combined with Set Height. Publishing sends your GIF to the vhs.charm.sh servers. The README does not state a license beyond a link to an MIT LICENSE file, which I did not open.

judge.reason: VHS turns terminal demos into editable, reproducible tapes, with CI-friendly text snapshots—a neat bridge between executable documentation and testing.

entry.title: vhs
entry.tldr: Write a plain-text script of typed commands and VHS plays it in a hidden terminal and renders a GIF, so demos can be regenerated like code.
entry.deeper_look:
VHS reads a `.tape` file, a list of instructions such as Type, Enter, Sleep, Wait and Set. It runs them in its own virtual terminal, captures frames, and writes the result named by the tape's Output line. GIF is the default. The README also lists MP4, WebM, a directory of PNG frames, and `.txt` or `.ascii` text output.

The README frames the purpose as "Write terminal GIFs as code for integration testing and demoing your CLI tools." A demo kept as a versioned text file can be diffed, reviewed and regenerated in CI, instead of being re-recorded by hand every time the tool changes.

The idea underneath is that a terminal session is just a deterministic sequence of input and output, so it can be treated as a test fixture. The README points to a golden-file workflow: commit the `.ascii` or `.txt` output and compare it between runs. Wait takes a regex, so a recording can sync with a spinner or prompt, and Hide/Show keeps setup steps out of the frame.

If you would rather not write a tape from scratch, `vhs record` captures a live session into one that you can then hand-edit. There is also a built-in SSH server, so a tape can be sent to a remote VHS host and a GIF comes back.
entry.install:
brew install vhs
# needs ttyd and ffmpeg on PATH; the brew formula lists both as dependencies
# alternatively, the official Docker image bundles the dependencies

entry.whats_unique: It makes a terminal demo a text file you can version and regenerate, with Wait on a regex and text output for golden-file comparison, which most screen recorders cannot do.
entry.caveats: It needs ttyd and ffmpeg on PATH, Linux and Windows need extra setup per the README, and the SSH server exposes the host's commands unless you restrict authorized keys.
